claim: TTB, tallying and regression are within about one point of each other out-of-sample on the classic ABC data sets; TTB uses 2-6 cues instead of all. The edge over regression is tiny (+0.3 points, city task) and becomes -0.4 on 63 data sets at 50% training. Table 2 of Gigerenzer & Goldstein 1996 re-checked: TTB .658, weighted tallying .658, regression .657, tallying .656, linear models .621-.623; regression there was fit in-sample.
agent_test: Compare a stop-at-first-decisive-check direct-mode rule against a weighted full checklist at equal tokens on S0-class items; log accuracy and tokens.
audit_note: Minor: Table 2 values, in-sample regression (given all Appendix information), +0.3 city task (72.2 vs 71.9 cross-validated, Wikipedia secondary) and -0.4 on 63 data sets (.743 vs .747, 50% training) verified; the 2-6 cues figure is not in any listed line (the evidence says 2.4 cues on average over 20 sets) and the Gigerenzer 2012 source was not opened.

claim: Less-is-more is a small-sample effect from bias versus variance: simple rules win when training data are few or noisy, and the advantage shrinks or reverses as data grow (TTB beats regression at 20 training cases, reverses at 100). An LLM-feature pipeline shows the same crossover: unit-weight vote beat learned weights when positives were few, with a knee near 100 positives (rho -0.50 and -0.38).
agent_test: Measure the direct-mode rule against the full routine as the S0 class record grows (n = 5, 20, 100 past cases); expect a crossover.
audit_note: Minor: the 20-vs-100 reversal is one house-price data set (22 houses, 231 pairs) in Parpart et al., not a general result, and the Gigerenzer 2012 bias-variance source was not opened; Parpart, Simsek and Griffin rho -0.50/-0.38 with knee near 100 positives all confirmed.

claim: Parpart et al. (2018) show that tallying and TTB are limits of Bayesian inference under infinitely strong priors; in simulations on the 20 ABC data sets an intermediate-strength prior that uses all cues (half-ridge) beat directed tallying and sign-constrained regression at every training size, and the COR model with a TTB rule usually peaked at intermediate priors (appendix). Strong bias helps, not simplicity itself; this rests on one paper.
agent_test: Let the S0 record shrink an answer toward a default but still let later checks override (partial pooling) versus a hard stop.
audit_note: The half-ridge result (intermediate prior best on all 20 data sets) is against directed tallying and sign-constrained regression, not TTB and unconstrained regression; TTB appears only in an appendix COR analysis (peak usually in the middle), and the two Parpart lines are one paper while Simsek tests no priors.
claim_before_audit: Pure heuristics are the infinite-prior limit; an intermediate-strength prior that uses all cues beats both TTB and full regression on the 20 ABC data sets (simulation). Strong bias helps, not simplicity itself.

claim: The environment decides: TTB is perfect only with non-compensatory weights and a correct cue order; in compensatory worlds equal-weight or hybrid rules win; with error TTB barely beats a dominance baseline.
agent_test: Classify items as one-decisive-check or many-weak-checks and route to stop-early or integrate; compare with a fixed policy.
audit_note: b04 and b05 are the same Hogarth and Karelaia paper (full text could not be opened, only abstracts via search confirm TTB effectiveness with 3-5 binary cues, hybrids better in compensatory worlds, and little advantage over a dominance rule under error); a14 only defines non-compensatory and does not test TTB; the only-with-perfect-order phrasing is not checked against the full text.

claim: Finding the best cue order for a lexicographic rule is hard to approximate (no efficient algorithm within any constant factor unless P differs from NP; Schmitt and Martignon 2006), and a greedy ordering is proven to do better than take-the-best validity ordering. Empirically (Simsek and Buckmann 2015) greedy is identical or very close to the best order on 63 data sets and validity ordering is very close to greedy except in a handful; on the German cities set fitting accuracy was .758 best, .756 greedy, .742 validity (1.6 points).
agent_test: Order direct-mode checks by recorded hit rate versus greedy conditional ordering at equal tokens.
audit_note: The .758/.756/.742 (1.6-point) figures are from one earlier German-cities data set cited by Simsek and Buckmann, not 63 real data sets; across the 63 sets validity ordering is described only as very close to greedy except in a handful, and the paper says continuous cues placed first mask ordering differences (relative accuracy of the orderings drops more in the dichotomized versions), the opposite of validity losing most with continuous cues.
claim_before_audit: Finding the best cue order is NP-hard to approximate, but plain validity ordering is within about 1.6 points of the best on real data and greedy ordering is slightly better; validity loses most with continuous cues.

claim: Reliance on recognition rises with recognition validity across environments (r = 0.64 over 11 environments, p = .03; adherence 64-96% by task) and falls when the source is artificial or the criterion is known.
agent_test: Use seen-before/familiarity in the S0 class record only when its past hit rate is above 0.5 for that class; test with induced familiarity.
audit_note: r = 0.64 (p = .03, 11 environments), Pohl 89% to 75% and the 64%-96% table range check out, but b10 and b12 are the same Pachur et al. paper and Gigerenzer and Goldstein 2011 (b07/a13) share authors with it (the recognition-heuristic group) and report a different correlation (r = .57 across experiments).

claim: Whether people use recognition strictly non-compensatorily is contested: proponents report 23-97% always following recognition depending on lab; model-comparison studies find mostly compensatory integration (77.5% PCS with cues shown, 62% with cues from memory). Glockner & Broder re-checked against the PDF: N = 80, TTB 12 (15%), RHe 4, PCS 62 (77.5%); cues were shown, not retrieved.
agent_test: Test a hard-stop versus a soft-weight use of familiarity in the agent at equal tokens.

claim: The recognition-based less-is-more effect is mostly shown by simulation; it is predicted frequent but small (about 0.01-0.02 accuracy), is often not found empirically, and its demonstrations are disputed.
agent_test: Low priority. Only check that adding more recalled cases never lowers agent accuracy.

claim: Equal-weight or unit-weight rules predict nearly as well as fitted weights out of sample in social-science data (Dawes 1979: unit weighting is robust) and, per Czerlinski et al. as summarised by Gigerenzer 2012, on 20 ABC data sets under cross-validation; in the in-sample-favoured GG96 German-cities competition tallying (.656) was level with regression (.657), which had more information. An LLM yes/no checklist counted with unit weights matched or beat elastic-net weights when positives were scarce (RRF, F0.5 .102 vs .080, not separable at founder level). The median of 12 LLMs matched a human crowd (Brier .20 vs .19) but was worse than the best single model (GPT-4, .15).
agent_test: Replace weighted scoring of candidate answers by equal-weight voting at equal tokens. Expect the vote to lead below about 100 labelled positives and to tie above it.
audit_note: GG96 tallying .656 vs regression .657 is not an out-of-sample test (regression was given all Appendix information, more than any competitor), so it cannot support the out-of-sample wording; Schoenegger numbers (Brier .20 vs .19, p=.85; GPT-4 .15), RRF F0.5 .102 vs .080 and Dawes unit-weight robustness hold, though the ensemble aggregate is a median and Dawes full text could not be fully read.
claim_before_audit: Equal-weight or unit-weight rules predict nearly as well as fitted weights out of sample in social-science and ABC data (Dawes 1979 opened; GG96 tallying .656 vs regression .657), and an LLM yes/no checklist counted with unit weights matched or beat elastic-net weights when positives were scarce (RRF, F0.5 .102 vs .080, not separable at founder level). Pooling 12 LLMs with equal weights matched a human crowd but not the best single model.

claim: 1/N allocation was not consistently beaten by 14 optimising portfolio models on 7 data sets; sample mean-variance needs about 3000 months of data for 25 assets (abstract-level, unopened).
agent_test: Analogy only: try an equal split of token budget across sub-checks versus a fitted split.

claim: Fast-and-frugal trees (about 2 cues) match logistic regression, random forest and nearly SVM on held-out balanced accuracy on small real data sets (0.83, 0.83, 0.83 vs SVM 0.86), and beat standard instruments in some clinical and legal cases.
agent_test: Build a 1-3 cue tree with exits from the S0 class record; compare with the full routine on held-out items. Data sets were chosen by the authors.
audit_note: Minor: FFTrees paper confirms SVM 0.86 vs FFT/RLR/RF 0.83 on ten real data sets (not all small; SVM failed on two); the clinical and legal wins (Green and Mehr, Dhami bail) come from the Gigerenzer and Gaissmaier review, which I only knew from the listed lines and did not re-open.

claim: Longer or forced chain of thought lowers LLM accuracy on some tasks where deliberation also hurts people (Liu et al. 2024: up to 36.3 points lower for o1-preview vs GPT-4o on implicit statistical learning; lower CoT accuracy also on face recognition) and on unanswerable Knightian items (Bogdan 2026, single pre-registered study: 17.3 points, CI 7.7-25.5, strong in mid-to-large models, absent or reversed in the weakest); longer reasoning budgets also lowered accuracy on several task families (Gema et al. 2025). Two other labs report related but different findings: reasoning models write chains at least as long on unanswerable as on answerable items (Tsvilodub et al. 2026) and much longer responses on missing-premise questions (Fan et al. 2025); the 17.3-point size has not been replicated.
agent_test: Run direct versus CoT at equal tokens on S0-class items and gate deliberation by task class. Bogdan's size is single-author; the direction has support from Fan 2025 and Tsvilodub 2026 on small open-weight and 2025 reasoning models, not on 2026 frontier models.
audit_note: Numbers check out (36.3 points is the abstract maximum, an o1-preview vs GPT-4o comparison on one task; 17.3 points CI 7.7-25.5 from one pre-registered single-author study), but Tsvilodub et al. and Fan et al. are different experiments (chain length vs answerability, abstention rates only inferred from the abstract), not replications of the accuracy drop, and the effect is absent or reversed in the weakest models.
claim_before_audit: Longer or forced chain of thought lowers LLM accuracy where deliberation also hurts people or the question is unanswerable (implicit learning and face recognition up to 36.3 points; Knightian items 17.3 points; inverse scaling in test-time compute). Direction replicated by two other labs on matched unanswerable or missing-premise items (reasoning models write longer chains and abstain less); the 17.3-point size is not replicated.

claim: Chain of thought gives large gains mainly on math, symbolic and logic tasks (+14.2, +12.3, +6.9) and little elsewhere (56.8 vs 56.1); up to 95% of the MMLU gain is on questions containing an equals sign.
agent_test: Use a cheap maths/symbolic yes-no check to choose direct or deliberate mode; measure at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: Sprague et al. give symbolic +14.2, math +12.3, logical +6.9, so the claim lists math/symbolic in swapped order; 56.8 vs 56.1, 110 papers, and up to 95% MMLU equals-sign share all confirmed; Liu et al. only supports the CoT-can-hurt side.

claim: o1-like models overthink easy problems (about 20x the tokens of conventional models); self-training for shorter reasoning roughly halves tokens at unchanged accuracy on one base model.
agent_test: Cap reasoning on easy S0-class items and compare accuracy per token.

claim: Stop-at-sufficient LLM cascades cut cost with little accuracy loss across teams: FrugalGPT up to 98% less cost (2023), MoT cascade 40% of GPT-4 cost at 0.929 vs 0.931 accuracy, UCCI -31% at fixed F1 (2026), cascade routing +8% (cascading) and up to +12% (routing) over prior methods. Savings shrink to 30-60% outside the best case, and all depend on an accurate sufficiency signal.
agent_test: Cheap-first answer with a calibrated confidence gate before escalating to the full scaffold; measure cost at fixed accuracy. No 2026 frontier-price replication yet.
audit_note: Minor: all cited numbers verified (98%, 40% cost at 0.929 vs 0.931 is from the listed lines, UCCI -31% CI 27-35% at micro-F1 0.91, cascade routing up to 8%/12% as AUC gains over cascading/routing); the 30-60% savings range outside the best case is a synthesis (MoT 60%, UCCI 31%) and ignores FrugalGPT HEADLINES at about 80%; the 12-LLM-free MoT accuracy figures were not re-opened beyond the abstract.

claim: Frontier LLMs acting as investment advisors lean on one or two inputs (risk tolerance 57-88% of predictive weight), a one-reason pattern nobody prompted.
agent_test: Ablate single inputs to check the agent does not ignore later-listed ones. Source has no ground truth, so it shows sensitivity, not error.

claim: LLMs show human-like heuristic and bias patterns (anchoring, conjunction, outcome-based play), but newer models lose the intuitive trap answers on CRT (GPT-4 0% trap vs 55% humans); evidence is old-model and small-sample.
agent_test: The heuristics-and-biases subfield owns this. Old-model results do not carry over.

claim: No published study prompts or tests an LLM with take-the-best, recognition, tallying or fast-and-frugal trees as the explicit target; the nearest are Bogdan 2026 (CoT length) and its theory link to TTB. Re-searched in this run (arXiv API, about 12 queries): still no direct hit. The closest are a unit-weight LLM checklist (Random Rule Forest) and popularity-routing (PopQA).
agent_test: New experiment: TTB-style prompt versus weighted-sum prompt versus plain on cue-based judgement items at equal tokens. Absence claim rests on one search log.

claim: Frugal is not always fast: told to use TTB under a 2000 ms deadline, people complied less and were slower than with tallying in one experiment; the order reversed in another.
agent_test: Not applicable to LLMs beyond token cost.

claim: Bogdan proves truncating after k cues is optimal under heavy-tailed precision priors, equal to TTB when validities descend and to tallying when uniform (26,696 numerical comparisons, 0 mismatches). Recognition and trees only conjectured.
agent_test: Theory, unreviewed, single author. Do not build design on it.

claim: LLM-generated task priors let a small meta-learned model reproduce human use of rank-based rules in paired comparison (posterior model frequency 0.73 with two attributes).
agent_test: Cognitive-model study with no agent loop; a route to building environment priors only.

claim: Gigerenzer & Goldstein 1996 Table 2 checked: on the 83 German cities, TTB .658, weighted tallying .658, regression .657, tallying .656, unit-weight linear .621, weighted linear .623, Minimalist .647. TTB searched 2-20 cue values versus all. Regression was in-sample with full population data. The two linear models lose only because the recognition principle is not built in.
agent_test: Report accuracy margins at one decimal and tokens used; do not claim TTB beats regression.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-27 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: For an LLM, a learned weighting pays only after about 100 labelled positive cases; below that a unit-weight count of yes/no checks is the lower-variance choice (knee near Npos = 100; effect tracks positives, not class ratio). Parpart's human-data crossover was 20-100 cases.
agent_test: Grow the S0 class record to 10, 30, 100 labelled cases; compare a count-of-checks rule with fitted weights at each size.

claim: Entity popularity is a measurable recognition-validity cue for LLMs: correlation with accuracy about 0.4 for GPT-3 davinci-003 and about 0.1 for GPT-Neo 1.3B; a popularity threshold as a retrieval gate gave 46.5% (+5.3 points over non-adaptive) and let the large model skip retrieval on 60% of questions. Models also carry an internal known-entity signal that causes refusal versus hallucination.
agent_test: Measure the agent's own recognition validity on the S0 class (known versus unknown entity) and test whether it follows familiarity when other cues contradict.
audit_note: Minor: 46.5% (5.3 points above any non-adaptive method) is GPT-3 with GenRead+Contriever whereas the 40% retrieval rate (skip on 60%) is davinci-003 with BM25, so they are separate configurations; correlations about 0.4 and 0.1 confirmed; Ferrando et al. abstract confirms the entity-recognition directions are causal for refusal vs hallucination.

claim: Learned or classifier routing between direct and reasoning modes cuts tokens by 41-76% at near-equal accuracy where item difficulty varies (MATH-500 .78 vs .79 at 2,811 vs 4,796 tokens; GSM8K -76% tokens; MMLU-Pro +10.2 points at -48.5% tokens against an unclear baseline) but gains vanish when difficulty is uniform and a wrong route is costly (NoThink-only 12 points lower on MATH-500).
agent_test: Route S0-class items with a cheap test; record routing accuracy and the accuracy lost per misroute.

claim: Independent labs see the cost of long reasoning on unanswerable items: reasoning models write chains at least as long on unanswerable as on answerable items (85% posterior probability that they are longer) and abstain credibly worse than they answer (beta 0.96) and worse than humans (beta 1.03), with the answer-abstain gap larger in reasoning than instruction-tuned models (beta 1.67) (Tsvilodub et al. 2026); an efficiency reward raised abstention 14.7% and cut chains 44% on average in fine-tuned 4B/8B models; Fan et al. 2025 independently report much longer responses by reasoning models on missing-premise questions.
agent_test: Add an early answerability check before any long chain; count tokens spent on unanswerable items.
audit_note: Betas are mislabelled: 0.96 is abstention below answering accuracy, 1.03 is the human comparison, and 1.67 is the question-type by model-type interaction (answer-abstain gap larger in reasoning than instruction models); Fan et al. report longer responses on missing-premise items but abstention rates only inferred from the abstract.
claim_before_audit: The cost of long reasoning on unanswerable items is seen by independent labs: reasoning models write chains at least as long on unanswerable items and abstain worse than humans and than instruction-tuned versions (beta 0.96 and 1.67); an efficiency reward raised abstention 14.7% and cut chains 44%.
